title: Tasting the Flavor
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch's main teaching is that even in the midst of life's challenges and mundane routines, we have the opportunity to cultivate gratitude and appreciation for the present moment. By recognizing that things can lose their flavor over time, we can learn to approach our experiences with curiosity and compassion, rather than trying to escape or numb them. This involves embracing the beauty in difficult situations, such as illness or boredom, and finding ways to add flavor back into our lives when they become stale.
topics: koan (not explicitly mentioned but implied in the context of "exhibits in a museum")

sentences.text: If you'd like, you could circle in, get a little closer.
Chanting the chant before dharma talks is always very moving, to think of actually tasting the truth of Buddha's words.
As many of you know, I'm in the process of becoming a lay teacher, and it's very moving to think that this is what I will do, this is what I want to do.
And yet it's also an incredible, beautiful responsibility to be true to Buddha's words, so I'll do my best.
My talk tonight went through many transformations.
It started out about a month ago with a little girl in my doctor's office.
I was sitting in my PCP or general practitioner's office waiting for my usual med check, and he's a very good, a very busy doctor, so I usually pack a lunch and a good book.
He sees families and children, and this little girl came over to where I was sitting and just started chatting me up.
She told me all about the preschool she went to, and she was chewing this gum that she said her grandma had given her.
After a few minutes she suddenly stopped and took it out of her mouth and said, "It's lost its flavor."
She just took it and threw it in the trash, and that started a whole rolling of thoughts in my mind about what it means when something loses its flavor.
She was so comfortable with simply letting go of it, not being upset.
Lost its flavor, not expecting any more from it, just lost its flavor, it's time to go.

So it made me think: what do I do when flavor goes out of things, out of relationships that I start to take for granted, out of work that I've been doing for so many years I could almost do it in my sleep?
Which is horrible when you think I'm a therapist and I care very deeply for my clients, and yet sometimes I wonder if I've lost a bit of the spark.
What do we do when the things that used to bring us joy don't do that anymore?
Throw it away?
I certainly think in that little girl's case she handled it beautifully.
She just accepted that it was done, she was done with it, end of story.
But there are so many meanings to that word flavor, and in our disposable culture, what I see as our disposable culture, it's pretty easy to get rid of things that have lost their flavor.
Although it's not so easy with jobs anymore.
I think we're all pretty protective of our jobs now.
It didn't always used to be that way.
I remember when my father, who's 88 now, was a professional in the 50s and 60s, you switched jobs, you climbed the ladder, you moved up, there was no concern.
At least, I'm sorry, that's very classist, at least for the college-educated professional classes.
If this job was no longer enough or whatever, you could move on, and if you were good, you were pretty much guaranteed of getting another job.
I realize it's not so easy in our economy.
But when I talk about a disposable culture, I think about how many marriages end in divorce, how many people just expect to break up.
If it doesn't work anymore, you just stop and change.
And then I thought of what comes very close to home for me, and that is: what do I do when Zen practice loses its flavor for me?
I've struggled with that for years now.
There are times when I know it is the richest thing in my life, and there are other times when I have felt distant and bored and not wanting to sit and let what comes up come up.
In my 18 years or so, I've dropped out a few times, especially in the beginning.
I go away.
Part of it is that I felt I had to sit hard, I had to sit like the big guys, I had to not do a chair, I wanted to sit without moving, and I have arthritis, so that's pretty impossible to do.
My ego took the heart and made it difficult for me sometimes to be here comfortably, and it's taken me a long time.
Tim mentioned to me in a personal conversation a few weeks ago, "I haven't seen you lie down in the Zendo in a while."
That's something our guiding teacher Norman gave me permission years ago to do.
He said, "Whatever keeps you practicing, lie down, whatever."
It was actually just Monday, I had a lot of pain in my back and I finally laid down for my practice.
I thought, yeah, whatever keeps you practicing.
It's not about the exact posture, although I think it's certainly important to pay attention to your posture, and the uprightness that brings everything upright, opens your heart.
One of the things that made this talk change a few times is an article that was recommended to me a while ago by Marty Bartlett.
It's called "Lost Love in Anxious Times," an incredible article by Norman Fischer, printed in Shambhala Sun, September 09.
I read that and I thought, oh, there's so much to apply to the same issue of flavor, when life loses its flavor or when life loses its joy because of so much loss, so much anxiety.
And then just today I got an email from a friend of mine I hadn't heard from in a while.
It turns out I hadn't heard from her because her little four-year-old, while they were vacationing up at Mt.
Baker, was on an upper bunk bed and fell and broke her neck.
She had to be ambulanced and then medivacked to Harborview.
Some of you may know this family I'm talking about.
I told them I wouldn't mention names, but so you know.
They almost lost their other little girl a few years ago, their 11-year-old, who about five years ago contracted some very, very rare, strange blood disease that almost killed her.
She was down at Children's for three months in ICU.
Actually it was four years ago, because at that time my friend gave birth to this other little girl, who was born with hip dysplasia.
The older girl, after a lot of very tough treatment, got better.
She got cured as far as we know.
She's cured, and it's wonderful to see her play soccer and run around again.
Her little baby sister was in this [unclear: "hip race"] for her first two years of life to fix the hip dysplasia, and she adapted to it.
I guess babies don't think, okay, this is what I do.
So she learned to crawl.
I remember going to her big sister's soccer game and she just crawled over to me and raised her hands so I'd help her up, and she'd hang onto my leg.
This incredible [unclear: "hip race"] would certainly be daunting to a lot of us.
So she got out of that after two years and was doing really well, and now this happened.
The letter from my friend was very [unclear: "popular"] and very positive.
She says, "We find ourselves so deeply filled with gratitude for so many things."
The little girl actually has a halo, a round wire screwed into her neck to hold her head tight, and she's coping with it.
My computer's not very good, but she's on her trike with it.
It's like she's [unclear: "into fatigue-able"].

But anyway, the mom says, "We are so grateful that there is a medical system that has such a thing that comes in such small sizes that can fit your four-year-old, and that there are people trained to interpret x-rays and install devices like the halo.
And that we actually have, incredibly expensive as it is, insurance that will cover the majority of this phenomenal expense of having your child down in Harborview for a month and home."
They're grateful for the doctors and the nurses, the helicopter pilots, the flight nurses, all the people that kept this little four-year-old together.

And then she also says, of course, the friends in her life who prepared dinners for them and took care of their house while they were gone, even did their laundry while they stayed in the hospital with her.
They see this really terrible thing as a very wonderful thing to be grateful for.

And she finishes up, "P.S., when you see a little girl, ask her who else wears halos besides angels, and she'll say, 'Me.'" She's taking that very constrictive device as well as she did her hip dysplasia device.
It's just incredibly beautiful.
So the theme of my talk was going to be about loss and love and how to deal with this in these anxious times.
Originally I was going to do it before Bob's [unclear: "shoe sew"] period, but since he did grief so well, I waited.
And actually I don't want to focus so much on the loss, although I know I've been talking about some sad stuff here.

What impresses me most, about Norman's article and about my friend's little girls who have been through more [unclear: "medical health"] than I can even imagine, and I was, a, quote, crippled kid, is that they still have love and joy and want to live.
It's just so moving, so moving.

So when I think about how small a person can be sometimes, when I think about how such and such has sort of lost its flavor, or I'm not interested in that anymore, or this is hard or it's boring, instead of sitting with it and looking at what this boredom is really about...
As a psychologist I know that boredom is a cover-up.
Boredom is a patina you paint over your feelings so that you don't see what you're feeling and you certainly don't feel them.
It's a big red flag.
When you're shedding something so powerful and beautiful as Zazen, to feel bored, I think, is a big red flag that you're not feeling something.
So how do we each deal with it when something, metaphorically, we put it in our mouth and decide, eh, I don't know if this has its flavor anymore?
Do we throw it away?
Do we create that patina over it and say, well, this is just the whole thing, it's just boring, it's just not to be explored?
I know how easily I can look at other people and see their faults, and when they're not like me but I want them to be.
But I can sweeten the flavor by trying to find our commonalities, by noticing the beauty of just their human skin, their eyes, their smile.
Nature, of course, in all its different seasons and dresses, it's easy to look at that and think, how can that possibly lose its flavor?
How could I let it lose its flavor?
But I also know that sometimes I feel I must deaden it.
I have to turn away from the beauty, from everyone, when I feel there's something terribly wrong and not to be looked at.
So I'll turn away, I won't let anyone touch me or comfort me or cheer me up.
I deaden myself to the flavor they're offering to rejuvenate me, and it's fear, it's fear of looking at my own feelings.
Flavor in terms of life is not really passive, although I think we often see it that way.
I know I struggle with that, thinking yes, it is passive.
I didn't decide the flavors of my life.
I didn't decide to give myself this disease when I was a kid.
I didn't decide to give myself these wonderful parents who are now horribly sick, one who has lost her mind with Alzheimer's.
I didn't make this screwed-up economy, and I didn't make my practice hard because people in economic straits will put psychotherapy on the bottom of their list, right?
You've got to have a house and food and clothes first, and therapy is kind of at the bottom there, which means that therapists, at least some of us, aren't real busy these days.
And I think, well, I didn't choose that.
It's passive, passive ugly flavors that have been forced on me, and I don't want them and I don't want to think about them.
Wow, what a way to make myself into the world's biggest victim and feel powerless and helpless.
So why would I want to sit with those feelings?

Because sitting and breathing and just letting whatever comes up come up is sometimes kind of like your own private horror show, especially if you let it catch you and you follow it out, which is something I am working with: not getting caught.
Getting back to Norman's article, he actually borrows from a man named Michael Palmer, who said a beautiful thing about those personal horror shows in your mind.
Excuse me, my printer printed it out in the tiniest way I could get.
*There you are with all your demons, your repetitive negative themes.
Your mind, to borrow a phrase from the poet Michael Palmer, is a museum of negativity and you are sitting there quietly breathing inside this museum.
There's nothing else to do, you can't fix anything, you can't change the pictures on the wall.
The situation is beyond that and gradually it dawns on you*
that these dark thoughts and anxious, anxious feelings are just that.
They are thinking and feeling.
They are like exhibits in a museum of negative pictures, but not necessarily the real world beyond the museum.
We can certainly make it feel that way by saying, "This is the reality.
This museum in my head of this horror show is my reality."
But it's not.
It's thoughts and feelings and interpretations of what's coming to you in life.

When it dawns on you that these dark thoughts and anxious feelings are just that, exhibits in this museum, this simple insight that thoughts and feelings are just thoughts and feelings is slight but makes a world of difference.
You can continue to sit, continue to pay attention to body and breath, and you can label those things just like you would label a painting.
"This is the Madonna by whoever."
You can label them: thinking, thinking, feeling, feeling, memory, fear, thinking, feeling.
Eventually you are able to pick up your coat from the coat check and walk out of the museum into the sunlight.
In other words, they are not a place you have to stay.
It's not your prison.
It can be.
You can make it that.
I've made it that at times, but it doesn't have to be.

Perhaps sitting with exactly what you feel will show you that your mind can be just that, a museum of painful, ugly things that make you want to either paint it over, like I said, with that patina of boredom, or to say, "This is hell, why do I want to do this?"
Or to say, "This has lost its flavor for me and I need to seek elsewhere to not feel these feelings."
It doesn't work.
But being able to see that they are just thoughts and they are just feelings allows you to come and go from that museum.
You don't have to stay.

And outside, as my friend who has been through hell is so able to see, there is so much beauty in every single person who did their job on one level and yet also went out of their way to make sure her little girl's spinal cord was not severed, that they would protect that spinal cord and she would not have the paralyzing effects that could have come from a broken neck.
And to take joy in that, that people cared enough.
Lately I've had sort of a mixed feeling about science, as some of you know, because science is keeping my parents alive when the quality of their life is not what it was.
And yet my father has a choice to turn off the ventilator and he's choosing not to do it.
I believe he's choosing that because he sees my mother now has dementia or Alzheimer's, and when she remembers who he is, she begs him not to die and leave her.
They've been together 57 years and he honors his vows.

And I think he's honoring his vows by working with my family to make a room in their house, the same house I grew up in, into his own personal ICU so he can stay alive and communicate through writing on a whiteboard.
And sorry, I just lost my train of thought.
He could certainly have made, he has the legal document to check out.
He's making a choice not to.
He's making a choice to continue, as Norman actually said to me not too long ago when I was crying, saying, "Why doesn't he just die?
I don't want him to die, but I don't want to see him like this."
And Norman said, "He's choosing this suffering for a reason and you have to accept that."
That there can be conscious choices of suffering.
It's when we don't consciously choose, I think, that we truly suffer the kind of suffering that Buddha was talking about.
The suffering where we feel helpless, where we feel despair and don't see any way out.
That's a different thing than what my dad is choosing, and Norman really kind of helped clarify that for me.
I have so much material here.
I called Tim shortly before, saying, "I don't know how I'm going to get through all this," because what I really would like is for us to talk together about what we do when things lose flavor.
Not just the little things like, "I don't care for the color on this wall, I think I'll paint it chartreuse today."
But the big stuff: the relationships, the devotion to sitting, the devotion to our work, whatever we've chosen, the devotion to our children.
Like my father, his devotion to his wife.
What do we do?
So what I'd like us to do with the time we have is maybe break up into twos or threes and just consider these questions, if you would.
There's more material, and I'm probably going to be bringing it up at the next Saturday active listening group, just because it offers such good material to listen and speak about.
But if I can find my questions, I was never Hemingway-like in my writing.
So, as I said, what do you do when flavor goes out of the important things in your life?
How do you know when it's time to let go?
When it really is like that little girl, it's a piece of gum.
It can be a metaphor or it can just be a piece of gum.
It's a piece of gum that it's time to let go of and not worry about anymore and not fume and fret over.
It doesn't taste good anymore, and she had no problem with that.
It's gone.
And when is it time to rethink?
Has it really lost its flavor, or is it how I'm interpreting it?
Is it how I'm projecting something onto it?
Is it how, as somewhere here in Norman's article he talks about, we can fall so easily back into our defenses of childhood when really confronted with something difficult and painful?
How do we deal with that?
How do we keep from repeating those old patterns of pushing it away, blaming somebody else for it, pretending it's not happening?
There's a little bit of irony I found when I was thinking of just sitting and experiencing what I kind of call a numb pain.
It's pain that I can't quite put my finger on.
And I'm talking emotional pain here.
I can figure out the physical pain pretty easy, but the almost numbing pain of being overwhelmed with everything, and that personally, when I want to throw in the towel, what do you all do?
I know those are a lot of questions.
They're not terribly focused, but I'd kind of like them to be open-ended.
And we have quite a bit of time, so we could break into threes and talk about those issues.
Is this too foggy?
Would you like a little clarification?
Yeah.
So, okay, why don't I use the bell?
Why don't we just sit for a couple of minutes with all this material I've thrown out.
I don't even think it's half of it.
We'll sit for a few minutes and then we'll do the active listening, where each person will take five to seven minutes.
I'll ring the bell and we won't respond to each other.
We'll simply listen.
And if there's time at the end and there are things you'd like to say to what you've heard, we can do that then.
But this will be just the active listening.
But first let's sort of gather our thoughts.
Is there a way to turn this idea into a metaphor?
Anybody want to share?
Chris?
**Participant:** I thought that in my life I didn't feel like that chewing gum was losing its flavor.
It was hotter.
Did you flavor jelly beans?
Magical little jelly beans?
Sometimes you get cinnamon and sometimes you get nose blubber and sometimes you get root beer and sometimes bark, you know.
For me it's not losing flavor.
It's just sometimes having opinions about what the flavor should be like.
Yeah.
That really turned up a lot.

**Participant:** I don't feel like that, but what also struck me when you were talking, it is an incident that happened today at school at the end of the day, when you were reading the article and talking about the Museum of Thoughts, recognizing the impermanence of thoughts and those heavy feelings and seeing through that.
But I have a student who is schizophrenic.
She's 19 years old, and she had early onset schizophrenia normally.
She's 19 and she was having a severe aggravation.
It looks like this is going to be medication that's not working.
She's conscious, she knows what's going on.
And she came to us after school today, and she sits in the classroom and the walls will bleed on her or rats will come and attack her, and all this is going on throughout the day.
She came today and she just broke down and said, "Why should I live?
I have no value to the rest of the world.
I have no value to myself."
And just total despair.
And I think, I've lost all of my thoughts and my feelings as impermanent, as empty, in these ways.
But here's this person with this mind and body that she has, that I can't give her that consolation.
I can't say to her, "Well, it's a museum."
It almost seems like the place that I'm in, the place that we are in, it's a very gracious gift and it's a luxury, because there are so many people with all that going on in their lives.
And what?
Is it?
I don't know.
I don't know.
**Participant:** So that sure came to mind.
I was also, then, teacher Jack Duffy once said to me, you can't really do meditation if you're living on the street and you have no idea where your next meal is coming from.
You can, but it's harder to have that, I guess, trust that I'll get through this.
At the time it made a lot of sense to me.

He and I were both working with severely disturbed folks at the clinic when he said it's not something you can really offer somebody who's in the middle of a psychotic break and can't even, they're living on the street.
They can't maintain a rented subsidized housing.
But I don't know.
That's tough.
**Participant:** I think, like the analogy of things losing flavor, this is another Taylor saying: how do you put some spice in your life?
How do you add the flavor back?

That's what I'm working with, trying to add flavor back into my work so that I can, because like you said, everybody's clinging to their jobs and it's really hard to change jobs and careers at this time.
So what do you do to keep it fresh and keep it tasty and good?
I just thought that was a really good analogy.
And I'm picking up different jelly beans along the way too.

Some of them taste good and some of them don't taste so good, but it keeps it interesting and it helps me get through the days until things turn around and maybe a new door will open for me somewhere.
**Participant:** Yeah, I like that too. [unclear: "Bernie bots"], every flavor bean.
Yeah, sometimes it's cherry and sometimes it's vomit.
And you just don't know what you're going to get.

I'm not sure that things losing their flavor is necessarily going to get satiated on something and move on and try some other things that may now open us up to a whole new set of flavors and experiences.
Maybe it's just our natural progression or evolution through parts of our lives or our jobs or whatever, but there's some balance.
Certainly, if nothing had a flavor, that could be a pretty desperate position for a person to be in, pretty hopeless and in support.
But just because something loses its flavor, or it's time for a new job or a new task, I don't think is necessarily something that we need to avoid.
**Yuzan Nancy Welch:** Yeah, I can't remember.
It might have been Janet pointed this out when I was telling somebody this story about the little girl who just so easily let go of her gum.
I had seen it more, pondering, what are you doing?
Something loses its flavor.
And this person, who I can't exactly remember, I think it was Janet, said, "But sometimes it's time to let go."
And she just let go of it.
Like you say, sometimes it doesn't mean you're supposed to fix it or change it or spice it up.
It's time to let go and let the next natural progression of things happen.
Yeah.
